It is derived from NYgrid, the open New York model of the Anderson lab at Cornell (MIT License), at one pinned commit. The starting point is NYgrid's 140-bus NPCC case: New York and its neighbors. The file's header lists every change:

  • the changes of NYgrid's own modifyMPC.m: some bus types, loads made positive, three lines between PJM and Ontario removed, ten tie-line ratings and two lines added;
  • the fixed unit list of NYgrid's hourly case: thermal, nuclear and hydro units, the units of the neighboring regions, and the Hydro-Quebec import;
  • the units of zone J (New York City) split evenly over buses 81 and 82;
  • the 765 kV Massena-Marcy line, from bus 47 to bus 43.

The file is the network with the units' limits. It is not a solved operating point: the New York units are at zero output, and the loads and the dispatch come from the pool.

Of the 140 buses, 46 are in New York. Ten of the 227 branches have a rating. There is no HVDC link, and the base is 100 MVA.

docs.title: The zone column says where a bus is
docs.text:
Zone code Where Buses 1 to 11 the NYISO load zones A to K 46 12 New England 36 13 Ontario 31 14 MISO 10 15 PJM 17

The file is one system, so it has one area: the bus area column is 1 on every row. The package reads a bus's region from the zone column. A zone outside 1 to 15, or an area other than 1, is refused. The codes and their names are in constants/newyork.py (ZONES, REGIONS).

Beyond MATPOWER's own fields the file has mpc.bus_name, mpc.genfuel, mpc.bus_latlon (degrees) and mpc.gen_ramp (MW per minute). It has no mpc.gencost.

pipelines/newyork/make_case.py is the recipe of the file: it makes the file again from NYgrid's Data/ folder. A test checks that the recipe still reproduces the shipped file exactly.

A change to the grid is an edit to the file, one row per line. No code patches the case on the way in. A variant in code is a copy, never a change in place: hvdc_links(case) or externals_at_base(case, base).

docs.title: What the reader refuses
docs.text:
Case.from_matpower reads the file with matpowercaseframes, the reader pandapower uses for .m files. A branch with status 0 is left out, and a tap ratio of 0, MATPOWER's mark of a line, is read as 1. A file whose parts disagree is refused with a DataConditionError that names the file and what is wrong:

  • a bus number that is not whole, or is on two rows;
  • a unit or a branch on a bus the case does not have;
  • a zone number outside 1 to 15, or an area other than 1;
  • an indexed assignment such as mpc.bus(1, 3) = 500;;
  • a field that is not one of the case's. The standard mpc.gencost, mpc.gentype, mpc.areas and mpc.dclinecost are passed over.

tests/nygrid/test_case_file.py has one test per rule.

docs.title: Areas in the code
docs.text:
The file has one area, but Case.area is derived from the zone code on read: 2 for a New York bus (NY_AREA), and the source model's own area number for each neighbor.

Zone code Case.zone Case.area 1 to 11 A to K 2 12, New England "" 1 13, Ontario "" 4 14, MISO "" 5 15, PJM "" 6

docs.title: Reading the file
docs.text:
In this package:

from fdia_graph.systems.case import CASE_FILE, Case, nygrid_case

case = nygrid_case()                    # the shipped file
same = Case.from_matpower(CASE_FILE)    # or any file laid out like it

In MATPOWER the file is an ordinary case function:

mpc = loadcase('case_nygrid');

In pandapower, build the net from the Case. PandapowerSolver does it (Solving):

from fdia_graph.data.pandapower_solver import PandapowerSolver

net = PandapowerSolver(case).net    # 140 buses, 271 generators

pandapower's own converter, from_mpc, fails on this file in pandapower 3.4.0. The converter has a bug on a branch that joins two voltage levels and has no rating, and the file has 83 of them. PandapowerSolver avoids it by giving every branch a placeholder rating.

docs.title: The other files of systems/
docs.text: File Holds fixes.py two variants of the New York case, each a copy: externals_at_base and hvdc_links ownership.py Ownership: the client that owns each bus; assign_clients gives each New York bus to its utility states.py PoolStates: solved voltages read frame by frame as the states a timeline walks tables.py the reader of the CSV input tables pandapower_types.py the pandapower net, named as types for from_pandapower

docs.title: Which systems have released datasets
docs.text:
System Released How to get a timeline the eight ieee systems a pool and a timeline of 72,000 frames each fg.load("ieee118") downloads it New York nothing yet build the pool (Build the operating points), then the timeline (Generate a timeline)

You can also generate your own timeline on any of the eight ieee systems with fg.generate (the tutorial).

docs.title: Analyse a timeline
docs.text:
This tutorial runs two analyses on one timeline: a state estimator, which recovers the state of the grid from the readings, and a localizer, which says which buses are under attack. Both run in seconds on a small timeline.

The analyses are in the second toolkit, fdia_analysis.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "fdia-analysis[se]"

This installs fdia-graph with it. The se extra adds pandapower and scipy, which the estimators need.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
The tutorial uses first_run, the timeline of Generate a timeline. A released dataset works the same way: replace the name with "ieee14".

import fdia_graph as fg

train = fg.load("first_run", split="train")
test = fg.load("first_run", split="test")

Fit on the train split and score on the test split. Pass the train split whole: both analyses calibrate on its benign frames.

docs.title: 1. Estimate the state
docs.text:
WLS is weighted least squares, the classical state estimator.

from fdia_analysis.se.methods import WLS

est = WLS().fit(train)
xhat = est.estimate(test)
print(xhat.shape)  # [n, 2N-1]

estimate reads the measurements only. Each row of xhat is one frame's state: the angle of every bus but the reference bus, in radians, then the voltage magnitude of every bus.

scores = est.score(test)
print(scores.benign)
print(scores.At)
print(scores.Am)

score compares the estimate with the clean layer, the true state, per attack family. The run measured for this page printed (rounded):

ErrorPair(angle_mae_deg=0.017, voltage_mae_pu=0.00012)
ErrorPair(angle_mae_deg=0.023, voltage_mae_pu=0.00017)
ErrorPair(angle_mae_deg=0.159, voltage_mae_pu=0.00183)

The error under the overload Am is several times the benign error. The readings of an attacked frame fit a false state, so the estimator returns that false state and reports nothing unusual. That is what makes these attacks hard to see.

docs.title: 2. Locate the attack
docs.text:
SwingThreshold is the simplest localizer. It flags a bus when its injection changes by much more than the bus's recent changes: the swing feature of the file.

from fdia_analysis.localization.methods import SwingThreshold

loc = SwingThreshold().fit(train)
flags = loc.localize(test)
print(flags.shape)  # [n, N], True where a bus is flagged

fit sets one threshold per bus on the benign frames, at a false-alarm target of 1 %.

report = loc.score(test)
print(report.benign.false_alarm_rate)
print(report.At.detection_rate)
print(report.Am.detection_rate)

The run measured for this page printed (rounded):

0.018
0.017
0.467

About 2 % of benign frames raise an alarm. The slow ramp At is flagged no more often than a benign frame: each of its steps is smaller than the load's own changes, so a threshold on the change cannot see it. The overload Am moves faster and is flagged in about half of its frames.

These are the numbers of one 2,000-frame run, shown to explain the output. The measured results are on the study pages.

docs.title: What the two results say
docs.text:
Analysis Reads On these attacks WLS the measurements returns the false state SwingThreshold the change from the frame before misses the slow ramp

Both attacks are built to pass the classical checks. The study pages measure what does better, on the full datasets.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Estimate the state: an estimator that beats WLS.
  • State estimation and Localization: every method, with results.
  • Layers and labels: which layers an analysis may read.

docs.title: Generate your first timeline
docs.text: This tutorial generates a small timeline on IEEE-14 and loads it. It takes about five minutes on a laptop.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "fdia-graph[generate,torch]"

The generate extra adds pandapower, which the generator uses to read the IEEE cases.

docs.title: 1. Generate
docs.text:
import fdia_graph as fg

if __name__ == "__main__":
    path = fg.generate("ieee14", name="first_run", frames=2000)
    print(path)

What this does:

  1. Downloads the pool. The IEEE-14 pool of operating points is a file of about 25 MB, downloaded once and kept in ~/.cache/fdia_graph. A pool is the true state of the grid at every frame.
  2. Walks 2,000 frames. It places attack episodes, designs each one, and writes every frame with meter noise.
  3. Writes one file and registers it under the name first_run.

Most of the time is the design of the overload attacks (measured per episode).

docs.title: 2. Load it
docs.text:
train = fg.load("first_run", split="train")
print(train.summary())

Summary(system=14, N=14, E=20, n=1200,
        families={'benign': 600, 'At': 300, 'Am': 300})

The train split is the first 60 % of the frames. Half of them are under attack, shared equally between the two families the generator makes.

Family What the attacker does At a false load that rises a little each frame Am the reported flow of two lines rises to their ratings 
episodes = train.episodes
print(episodes.length[:5])  # [60 60 60 60 60]
print(episodes.family[:5])  # codes: 5 is At, 7 is Am

Each episode is 60 frames. From here the file loads like a released one (Load a dataset).

docs.title: 3. Change a setting
docs.text:
The common settings are keywords of fg.generate. The others are fields of the settings models it takes.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    fg.generate(
        "ieee14",
        name="ramps_only",
        frames=2000,
        families=("At",),
        attacked_frac=0.3,
        ramp_len=30,
        seed=7,
    )

This one places only slow ramps, 30 frames each, on 30 % of the frames. With no overload attack to design it runs much faster. The settings tables list every setting.

A timeline is fixed by its settings, its seed and its pool: the same call writes the same file.

docs.title: The same on the New York case
docs.text: The New York case goes through the same generator, with the same settings and other data. Nothing is released for it, so you build its pool first. That needs a checkout of the repository, the [ny] extra and the Ipopt solver, and several hours of solving. Build the operating points has the steps, and Generate a timeline the build of the timeline from the pool.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Analyse a timeline: run an estimator and a localizer on the file.
  • Generate a timeline: the steps, and every setting.
  • The attack families: what the two families are.

docs.title: Load a dataset
docs.text:
This tutorial loads a released dataset and looks at it four ways: one record, one batch, one whole split and one window. It takes a few minutes, most of it the download.

A dataset is one timeline: the meter readings of one test system, frame by frame, with attacks placed in it and labelled per bus.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "fdia-graph[torch]"

The plain pip install fdia-graph is enough for summary(), export, windows and episodes. One record (step 2) and the batches (step 3) need PyTorch, and export(format="pandas") needs pandas.

docs.title: 1. Load
docs.text:
import fdia_graph as fg

train = fg.load("ieee14", split="train")
print(train.summary())

The first call downloads the IEEE-14 timeline, a file of about 87 MB, and keeps it in ~/.cache/fdia_graph. Later calls read the cached file. The eight released systems are "ieee14" to "ieee300"; the IEEE-118 file is about 730 MB.

summary() gives the system, the number of buses N and branches E, the number of frames in this view and how many belong to each attack family.

fg.load reads the static graph once and slices frames on request, so the whole file is never in memory.

docs.title: 2. One record
docs.text:
A record is one frame.

record = train[0]
print(record["node_x"].shape)   # [N, 4]
print(record["edge_x"].shape)   # [E, 2]
print(record["y"].shape)        # [N]
print(int(record["family"]))    # 0 is benign
Field Shape Holds node_x [N, 4] bus readings: voltage, P, Q, angle node_m [N, 4] 1 where a meter exists edge_x [E, 2] branch flow readings: P, Q at the from end y [N] 1 at each attacked bus family one number which attack; fg.FAMILIES names the codes

A reading with no meter is stored as zero, so read the mask node_m with node_x. The static graph is on the dataset, not on each record: train.edge_index ([2, E]), train.edge_attr ([E, 8], the branch properties) and train.ybus (the admittance matrix). The data dictionary lists every field.

docs.title: 3. One batch
docs.text:
loader = train.loader(batch_size=64)
batch = next(iter(loader))
print(batch["node_x"].shape)  # [64, N, 4]
print(batch["y"].shape)       # [64, N]
print(batch["edge_index"].shape)  # [2, E]

loader returns a PyTorch DataLoader. Each batch holds the per-frame fields stacked, and the static graph (edge_index, edge_attr) once.

docs.title: 4. One export
docs.text:
export returns a whole split at once.

arrays = train.export(format="numpy")
print(arrays["node_x"].shape)  # [T, N, 4]
print(arrays["y"].shape)       # [T, N]
print(arrays["family"].shape)  # [T]
Call Gives train.export() numpy arrays (the default) train.export(format="torch") torch tensors train.export(format="pandas") one data frame train.export(["node_x", "y"]) only those fields

Every frame comes in three layers. node_x is what the operator saw. benign is the same scan with the attack removed. clean is the true state with no noise.

metered = arrays["node_m"] == 1
attack = (arrays["node_x"] - arrays["benign"])[metered]
noise = (arrays["benign"] - arrays["clean"])[metered]
print(abs(attack).max(), abs(noise).max())

The two differences hold where a meter exists, which is why the snippet reads the mask.

Layers and labels explains the layers and which of them a detector may read.

docs.title: 5. One window
docs.text:
A timeline is in time order, so it can be cut into windows for a sequence model.

X, y = train.windows(W=24, stride=12)
print(X.shape)  # [n, 24, N, 4]
print(y.shape)  # [n, N]

Each window is 24 consecutive frames of node_x, and y marks a bus attacked at any frame of the window.

Argument Default Meaning W the window length in frames stride 1 the step between windows label "any" "any", "last" (the last frame's label) or "frame" ([n, W, N]) layer "node_x" "node_x", "benign" or "clean" per_bus False one sequence per bus: [n*N, W, 4]

The episodes of the view are a table:

episodes = train.episodes
print(len(episodes.onset))
print(episodes.onset[:3], episodes.length[:3])
print(episodes.family[:3])

docs.title: Options of fg.load
docs.text:
# one split: "train", "val" or "test"; None is every frame
fg.load("ieee14", split="test")
# a subset of the families
fg.load("ieee14", split="test", families=["At"])
# per unit and radians; the default is physical units
fg.load("ieee14", units="pu")
# the same frames as a shuffled record table
fg.load("ieee14", order="random", seed=0)
Option Default Meaning split None "train", "val", "test", or every frame families None keep only these families, by name or code units "physical" "physical" (p.u., MW, MVAr, degrees) or "pu" (per unit, radians) order "time" "time", or "random": a permutation fixed by seed format "torch" "torch", or "pyg" for torch_geometric records release None a data release such as "v0.8.1"; None is the pinned one preload False read the whole split into memory once heldout False keep As and Ar out of train and validation [BOY22] seed 0 the seed of the "random" order

windows needs order="time" and raises MissingCapability otherwise.

docs.title: What the released files hold
docs.text: The released files hold seven attack families on 72,000 frames per system, about half of the frames under attack. The current generator makes two of them, At and Am, with a different Am (The attack families). To get a file with the current families, generate one: Generate a timeline.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Generate a timeline: make your own dataset.
  • Analyse a timeline: run an estimator and a localizer on one.
  • Examples: three runnable baselines.

docs.title: Add a design family, an alarm rule or a test system
docs.text:
The package has three extension points. Each is a small base class or constructor of the package itself, not of one test system. This guide names each one, says what it must provide, and where it plugs in today.

You add You write Base A design family design(window, rng) AttackFamily An alarm rule first_alarm(stat) AlarmRule A test system a Case Case.from_pandapower, Case.from_matpower

Two runnable examples are in the repository under examples/nygrid/. They need no data, and the tests run both, so they stay current with the code.

docs.title: A design family
docs.text:
The design stage asks every family one thing: the episode of a window (EpisodeFamily.designed in src/fdia_graph/engine/attacks/family.py). Subclass AttackFamily, which answers that for you, and write design:

import numpy as np

from fdia_graph.engine.attacks.family import AttackFamily
from fdia_graph.models.plan import Episode


class MyFamily(AttackFamily):
    def design(self, window, rng):
        onset, vm, va = window
        ...
        return Episode(...)  # or None

What design receives. window is (onset, vm, va): the pool frame the window starts at, and the true voltage magnitudes (p.u.) and angles (degrees) over it, each [L, N]. rng is the random generator for this design.

What it returns. An Episode (models/plan.py), or None where the window holds nothing to attack.

Field of Episode Meaning family the family's name; it must be a name in fg.FAMILIES, whose code the file stores onset, length the window a the attack vector [L, M], one column per meter of the source's plan, added to each scan buses the buses it attacks, as the episode table records them clients the owners of the meters it moves; the file does not store it target_branch a branch it is anchored on, -1 for none; the file does not store it

The per-frame labels and tamper masks come from the vector itself: a meter is tampered where the vector moves its reading by more than its accuracy class, and a bus is labelled where a tampered meter sits. M and the place of each meter are the plan's, source.g.plan, which you can have before the source exists: MeterPlan.from_coverage(net.case, settings.meters, np.random.default_rng(seed)) is the plan a source with that seed draws.

Saying why there is no attack. When design returns None, set self.last_miss = "no_target" if the window held nothing to attack. design_explained then reports no_target. A None left unexplained reads as infeasible.

Refusing an onset. Return None at an onset the family will not take. The episode then moves to another free onset of its split, up to 20 times.

Keeping it stealthy. An attack the residual test should not see has to change the readings as h(x_false) - h(x_true) for a false state, as the package's own designs do (The attack families). A family that does not, like the example's slow bias, is the naive attack the residual test is meant to catch. It is useful as a baseline.

Where it plugs in. SearchSource, IeeeSource and SearchSource.for_pool take families=, a dictionary from a family's name to a family object:

source = SearchSource(grid, pool, settings, seed=1, families={"At": MyFamily()})

The key is "At" or "Am": your family takes the place of the search family of that name, and its episodes are placed with that name's length and share. source.generate(path) then places, designs and writes its episodes like the package's own. Episode.family must be a name in fg.FAMILIES; the file stores that name's code (Generate a timeline).

Example: custom_attack_family.py.

docs.title: An alarm rule
docs.text:
A rule turns a statistic per scan into the first scan it alarms on, or -1. The statistic can be a residual sum, a gap between two meters, or any score. AlarmRule is a protocol in the analysis toolkit, in se/detect/rules.py under analysis/src/fdia_analysis/. Any object with this method is a rule:

import numpy as np

from fdia_analysis.se.detect.rules import AlarmRule, PersistenceRule


class FirstOver:
    """Alarm at the first scan above a fixed level."""

    def __init__(self, level: float) -> None:
        self.level = level

    def first_alarm(self, stat: np.ndarray) -> int:
        hit = np.flatnonzero(np.asarray(stat) > self.level)
        return int(hit[0]) if len(hit) else -1


rule = FirstOver(3.0)
print(isinstance(rule, AlarmRule))          # True
print(rule.first_alarm([1.0, 2.0, 4.0]))    # 2

The package ships one rule, PersistenceRule: it alarms when k of the last n statistics exceed a threshold (2 of 3 by default), which a single noisy scan cannot trip.

benign = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=2000)
rule = PersistenceRule.fit(benign, q=99.9)
print(rule.first_alarm(benign[:300]))  # -1
  • Calibrate a rule on benign scans only. PersistenceRule.fit takes a percentile of benign statistics.
  • A rule fitted on no statistic at all raises NoBenignRecords, since it would never alarm.
  • Report a rule's false alarms on benign data beside its detection rate.

The package ships the rule and the protocol. The code that computes the statistic and asks the rule is yours. se/detect/__init__.py exports no name: import from rules.py.

Example: custom_alarm_rule.py.

docs.title: A test system
docs.text:
A test system is a Case (Test systems). There are two ways to make one of your own.

Call Takes Note Case.from_pandapower(net) a pandapower net with its power flow solved the general route Case.from_matpower(path) a MATPOWER case file needs the [ny] extra; the file must follow the New York file's conventions

Case.from_matpower reads a file laid out like case_nygrid.m: area 1 on every bus, and the zone codes of that file's legend (1 to 11 the NYISO load zones, 12 to 15 the neighbors). A file whose parts disagree is refused with a DataConditionError that names the file and what is wrong.

A SearchSource generates a timeline on any Network:

import numpy as np
import pandapower as pp
import pandapower.networks as pn

import fdia_graph as fg
from fdia_graph.data.profiles import RawSeries
from fdia_graph.generation.search import SearchSource
from fdia_graph.models.config import TimelineSettings
from fdia_graph.systems.case import Case
from fdia_graph.systems.network import Network

net = pn.case14()
pp.runpp(net)
grid = Network(Case.from_pandapower(net))

# a pool for this grid: [T, N, 4], one solved state per frame
hours = np.arange(300) / 60.0
profile = fg.load_profile(RawSeries(100 + 10 * np.sin(hours)))
pool = fg.generate_states("ieee14", profile)

settings = TimelineSettings.of(
    families=("At",), ramp_len=20, min_tamper=False
)
source = SearchSource(grid, pool, settings, seed=1)
path = source.generate("own_grid.h5")
print(fg.FdiaGraph(path).summary())

The example borrows the IEEE-14 pool builder, because pn.case14() is that grid. For a grid of your own you bring the pool. Two things hold for it:

  • fg.generate_states builds pools for the eight IEEE cases only.
  • A pool stores each bus's injection with load positive. The setting loads says how the designs divide it into load and generation: "scaled" for a pool made by scaling the case, "net" for a dispatched pool (How a pool's load is read).

One source generates one timeline. A second generate on the same SearchSource is refused; build a new source.

To change the New York grid itself, edit its case file (Test systems). Edit rows in place, or add and delete whole rows. A variant in code is a copy, never a change in place: hvdc_links(case), externals_at_base(case, base) (systems/fixes.py).

docs.title: What an extension should keep to
docs.text:
• Named errors. Raise the errors of fdia_graph.errors: ConfigError for a wrong argument, a DataConditionError for data that does not meet a condition, SolverUnavailable for an environment that cannot run the solver.
  • Settings are arguments. A setting is an argument of the function or constructor that uses it. A variant is a copy, never a change in place.

Changing the package itself is covered in Contributing.

docs.title: Generate a timeline
docs.text:
A timeline is the meter readings of one test system, frame by frame, with attack episodes placed in it. This guide generates one. It is the same guide for every test system: one method makes every timeline, and what differs between systems is settings and data.

Terms are in the glossary. Paths are under src/fdia_graph/.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A test system. One of the eight IEEE cases, or the New York case (Test systems).
  • A pool of operating points. One solved AC state per frame, in time order (Build the operating points).

For an IEEE case fg.generate downloads the released pool, so you need nothing else. For the New York case you build the pool first.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
TimelineSource.generate(out) in generation/source.py makes every timeline. Its body is short, and it runs these steps in this order.

A source is a subclass of TimelineSource. It builds the generator, the pool and the designer of its attack families, and it says what its files record. The package has one, in three spellings.

Source File Built on SearchSource generation/search.py a Network and a pool array IeeeSource generation/ieee.py an IEEE case by its name, and its pool array SearchSource.for_pool generation/search.py a Network and a pool file, as the New York case has

IeeeSource and for_pool build a SearchSource (The original generator on the New York case).

docs.title: 1. Open
docs.text:
Owner: TimelineSource.open, with TimelineWriter (generation/write.py).

The file is started beside out under a .part name. It takes the name out only when it is whole. A run that fails leaves no file, and a file already at out is left as it was. The writer stores the static graph first: the branches and what gives the admittance matrix.

docs.title: 2. Cut the splits
docs.text:
Owner: TimelineSource.cut_splits, with split_bounds and split_weeks in generation/plan.py.

The train, validation and test splits are cut before any episode is placed, so no episode is cut by a split. The setting split_by chooses how.

  • "time": three blocks in time order.
  • "week": whole weeks, drawn at random into the three splits, in strata of 20 weeks (split_weeks). This needs each frame's time.

Just before the cut the source runs prepare. It does nothing on a SearchSource; a subclass can work out there what it needs before the splits are cut.

docs.title: 3. Place
docs.text:
Owner: TimelineSource.place, with place_split in generation/plan.py.

Each split gets whole episodes at random onsets.

  • How many. The whole number of episodes whose frames come closest to attacked_frac of the split. The families share them so that each family gets about the same number of attacked frames (whole_episode_counts, largest_remainder).
  • Where. Longest first, each at an onset drawn uniformly among the positions where it fits. Episodes never overlap and none is cut (uniform_onset).
  • When it jams. A placement that cannot fit is retried whole 10 times (PLACE_TRIES). Then one episode of the family that jammed is dropped, recorded, and reported with a RuntimeWarning.

Adjacent episodes and long quiet stretches are outcomes of the uniform draw, not of a rule.

docs.title: 4. Design
docs.text:
Owner: TimelineSource.design, with SplitDesign and the source's Designer (generation/design.py).

The designer asks each family for the episode of a window: what the attacker changes on each frame (The attack families). An episode with no design at its onset moves to another free onset of its split, up to 20 times (REDRAWS). After that it is given up, recorded, and reported with a RuntimeWarning.

On a SearchSource the ramp At is the one family designed as the walk reaches it, because its design reads the frame before its onset. A ramp with no design therefore moves to a later onset only (Walk.relocate_later).

The designs of a split can run in several processes (workers). The file does not depend on the number of workers. The processes are spawned, so a script that asks for more than one worker must start under if __name__ == "__main__":.

docs.title: 5. Walk
docs.text:
Owner: TimelineSource.walk, with Walk.run in generation/emit.py.

Every frame is emitted in time order. A frame outside an episode is a benign scan: the readings of the pool state plus meter noise (Meters and noise). A frame inside an episode is that scan plus the attack. A frame of an episode whose own scan cannot be built is stored benign, and the file counts it in the attribute fallback_benign.

The walk writes a frame only after its split is placed and designed (planned_until in generation/plan.py). With split_by="time" each split is one block, so the walk writes that block next. With split_by="week" the weeks of the three splits alternate, so the walk stops at the first frame whose split is not designed yet.

docs.title: 6. Finish
docs.text:
Owner: TimelineSource.finish, with TimelineWriter.finish.

After the last frame the writer stores what the file carries besides its frames: the per-frame columns, the episode table, the attributes, and the temporal features where the file has them. The attributes record the settings as JSON (settings) with their hash (settings_hash), and per split and family the episodes requested, built, moved, dropped and short. Layers and labels says what each layer means, and the data dictionary lists every array.

docs.title: The settings
docs.text: Settings arrive as models from models/config.py. Each model checks its values when it is built, and a value it does not allow raises ConfigError.

docs.title: TimelineSettings
docs.text:
The settings of a SearchSource, so of every timeline the package generates.

Field Default Meaning attacked_frac 0.5 share of each split's frames under an episode families ("At", "Am") the families placed am_len None Am episode length in frames; None is the ramp's max_load_mw 2000.0 a larger load is never a target; None is off workers 1 processes that design the Am episodes split_by "time" how the splits are cut am_attack "overload" what an Am episode is; the one kind ramp RampSettings() the slow ramp At search SearchSettings() the attacker's area and the search overload OverloadSettings() the overload Am meters MeterSettings() the meter plan split SplitSettings() the three fractions

The sections:

Model Field Default Meaning RampSettings rate 0.002 At growth per frame RampSettings length 60 At episode length in frames RampSettings stealth_scale 1.0 multiplier on At's stealth bound SearchSettings hops 2 the attacker's reach in branches SearchSettings min_tamper True hold each At episode on the fewest devices SearchSettings min_budget 256 candidate supports solved per search SearchSettings area_rule "hops" how the attacker's area is chosen OverloadSettings rating_source "pool" "pool", "pglib" or "delta" OverloadSettings rating_margin 1.25 rating over the pool's peak flow OverloadSettings load_cap 0.5 largest shown load change, as a share OverloadSettings n_lines 2 lines one episode overloads OverloadSettings support_method "search" "search" or "rref" OverloadSettings rating_delta 0.10 with "delta": p.u. added to the target's true flow MeterSettings vbus_frac 0.6 share of buses with a voltmeter MeterSettings pmu_frac 0.2 share of buses with a PMU MeterSettings flow_frac 0.9 share of branches with a flow meter MeterSettings meter_model "hybrid" what the meters read SplitSettings fractions (0.6, 0.2, 0.2) train, validation, test

fg.generate and generate_timeline take a TimelineSettings, and also flat keywords that set one field each. A flat keyword is applied over the settings.

Flat keyword Sets attacked_frac, families, am_len, max_load_mw, workers, split_by the field of that name ramp_rate, ramp_len, stealth_scale ramp.rate, ramp.length, ramp.stealth_scale hops, min_tamper, min_budget the search field of that name redundancy meters (a MeterSettings) split split (three fractions, or a SplitSettings) am_attack "overload" sets am_attack; an OverloadSettings sets overload

seed (default 123) is an argument beside the settings. It fixes the meter plan, the meter biases and every attack draw.

from fdia_graph.models.config import RampSettings, TimelineSettings

settings = TimelineSettings(
    attacked_frac=0.3,
    ramp=RampSettings(length=30),
)
print(settings.lengths_for(("At", "Am")))  # {'At': 30, 'Am': 30}

docs.title: split_by and time=
docs.text:
split_by is a setting of every source.

Value The splits Needs "time" three blocks in time order nothing "week" whole weeks, drawn into the three splits each frame's time

The frames' times are the argument time=: numpy datetime64 values, one per frame, strictly increasing. Anything else is refused when the source is built. An IEEE pool stores no time, so an IEEE timeline split by weeks needs time= passed in. A New York pool stores its times.

With times, the file stores data/time, and no episode is placed across a gap in time. Without them, split_by="week" is refused with a ConfigError that says the pool carries no time.

docs.title: How a pool's load is read
docs.text:
A pool stores one net injection per bus. The search-based designs need the load and the generation behind it, and loads says how to divide it.

Value A bus's injection is read as For a pool made by "scaled" (default) the case's load and generation, both times one factor a power flow on a scaled case (the released IEEE pools) "net" all generation at a bus with a unit, all load at any other bus an OPF, which sets each unit's output on its own

Under "net" the load at a unit's own bus is not seen, so the designs never pick it, and a bus counts as a load only when its mean load over the pool is above 1 MW (LOAD_FLOOR_MW). The classes are ScaledSplit and NetSplit in engine/physics.py. A file records loads in its settings when it is not the default.

A design picks its targets among the grid's own buses (Case.own_bus). On an IEEE case that is every bus. On the New York case it is the 46 New York buses; the other 94 stand for the neighbouring grids.

docs.title: What differs between the IEEE cases and the New York case
docs.text:
One source generates both. Every row is a difference in data or in a setting. The steps above are the same.

Item IEEE cases New York case Case Case.from_ieee(n), the case pandapower ships nygrid_case(), a MATPOWER file in the package Load data one system load profile scales every bus a load per bus, from LoadModel Pool solve one power flow per step, in pandapower one OPF per frame in Ipopt, then one power flow A step that does not solve dropped from the pool kept in the pool, with an empty state; for_pool leaves it out of the timeline Frame times not stored in the pool stored in the pool loads "scaled" "net", set by for_pool Buses a design may target every bus the 46 New York buses Source IeeeSource, through fg.generate SearchSource.for_pool Released data a pool and a timeline per system none; you build both

The meter placement, the design families, the file layout and the defaults of TimelineSettings are the same on both. The attack families says what each design does.

docs.title: The original generator on the New York case
docs.text:
The New York case is a test case of SearchSource like an IEEE case: coverage meters, the search-based ramp and overload, and the settings of TimelineSettings. Reading the case file needs the [ny] extra. The pool is one you build (Build the operating points); the repository has a pool of two days for its tests.

from fdia_graph.data.pool import read_pool
from fdia_graph.generation.search import SearchSource
from fdia_graph.models.config import OverloadSettings, TimelineSettings
from fdia_graph.systems.case import nygrid_case
from fdia_graph.systems.network import Network

net = Network(nygrid_case())
pool = read_pool("tests/nygrid/data/days/pool_2019_v3_days.h5")
am = OverloadSettings(rating_source="delta", load_cap=0.1)
settings = TimelineSettings.of(split_by="week", ramp_len=12, attacked_frac=0.3, am_attack=am)
SearchSource.for_pool(net, pool, settings, seed=5).generate("out/ny_search.h5")

for_pool hands the generator the pool as it reads one: the solved frames only, with their times, injections positive for load, and loads="net". The file has the layout of an IEEE file: a flow at the from end, currents as real and imaginary parts, and the two temporal features.

On this case Meters MeterPlan.from_coverage draws them over all 140 buses, the neighbours' included Ramp targets New York buses with no unit whose mean load in the pool is above 1 MW Overload targets branches with both ends in New York; the units it may move are New York's A design's area the buses within hops of its targets, a neighbour's included: such a bus is never a target or a label, but its readings move with the false state Ratings rating_source="delta" rates a line from its own window; the default rates it at 1.25 times its peak flow in the pool

tests/nygrid/test_any_case.py runs this on the two checked-in days and checks that every labelled bus is New York's.

docs.title: A design family of your own
docs.text:
SearchSource, IeeeSource and SearchSource.for_pool take families=, a dictionary from a family's name to a family object. The object takes the place of the search family of that name, "At" or "Am". Its episodes are placed like that family's: the name must be in the settings' families, and the episode length is that name's (ramp_len for "At").

from fdia_graph.generation.ieee import IeeeSource
from fdia_graph.models.config import TimelineSettings

# X: a pool array [T, 14, 4]; MyFamily: a subclass of AttackFamily
settings = TimelineSettings.of(families=("At",), ramp_len=10, attacked_frac=0.3)
source = IeeeSource(14, X, settings, seed=5, families={"At": MyFamily()})
source.generate("out/own.h5")

A family that subclasses AttackFamily (engine/attacks/family.py) designs one attack vector per window, a value for every meter of the source's plan on every frame (Add a design family). Such an episode is designed before its split is walked. The file records it under the code of the family name its Episode carries. A meter is marked tampered where the vector moves its reading by more than the meter's accuracy class, and a bus is labelled where a tampered meter sits.

The designs of several workers run in spawned processes, so with workers above 1 the family object must pickle. tests/test_any_case.py runs a family of its own on IEEE-14.

docs.title: A timeline read as clients
docs.text:
SearchSource and SearchSource.for_pool take own=, an Ownership (systems/ownership.py): the clients' names and the client of each bus, -1 for a bus that belongs to none. Each meter then belongs to the client of its bus. The file records the names in the attribute client_names and each bus's client in graph/bus_client. The designs do not read the owners, so the attacks are the same with and without them.

import numpy as np

from fdia_graph.systems.ownership import Ownership

# net, pool, settings: as in the New York snippet above
case = net.case
bus_client = np.where(case.is_ny, np.arange(len(case.bus_id)) % 3, -1)  # three made-up clients
ties = bus_client[case.f] != bus_client[case.t]
own = Ownership(np.array(["a", "b", "c"]), bus_client, ties)
SearchSource.for_pool(net, pool, settings, seed=5, own=own).generate("out/ny_clients.h5")

assign_clients in systems/ownership.py builds the Ownership of the New York case from the utility territories and the bus locations among the build's inputs: each New York bus goes to the utility whose territory holds it.

The file opens with fg.FdiaGraph(path) like any timeline. Dataset (dataset/clients.py) is a second view of it, by meter and by client:

from fdia_graph.dataset.clients import Dataset

ds = Dataset("out/ny_clients.h5")
a = ds.client("a", split="train")
x = a.node_features()           # [T, N_c, 4]
op = ds.operator(split="test")  # every meter

A client sees only its own meters and the labels of its own buses. The operator view is the full scan. ds.clients lists the clients' names.

On a ClientView Shape Holds z [T, M_c] its observed scans, one column per meter it owns labels [T, N_c] the attack labels of its buses meters its rows of the meter table buses [N_c] the positions of the buses it owns frames [T] the frames selected; a week split has gaps node_features() [T, N_c, 4] voltage, angle, P, Q per bus; NaN where not metered temporal() [T, M_c] the change from the frame before On the Dataset Holds ds.plan the meter table, rebuilt from the file's masks (MeterPlan.from_masks) ds.z(frames) the flat reading vector of that table ds.z(frames, benign=True) the same scans without the attack ds.tampered(frames) the tampered meters

Dataset refuses a file that does not record its clients with NotATimeline. tests/nygrid/test_dataset.py writes such a file and reads it back.

docs.title: Entry point: an IEEE case
docs.text:
fg.generate loads the pool, generates the timeline and registers the file under a name.

import fdia_graph as fg

# needs fdia-graph[generate]
# downloads the IEEE-14 pool (about 25 MB) once
# about five minutes on a laptop
fg.generate("ieee14", name="my_run", frames=2000)
mine = fg.load("my_run", split="train")
Argument Default Meaning system "ieee14" to "ieee300", or the bus count name the name fg.load finds the file under frames None walk only the first frames of the pool states None your own pool: an array or a path out None the file's path; None is <name>.h5 in the cache seed 123 the seed settings None a TimelineSettings time None each frame's time

Without states, the pool is the path in $FDIA_GRAPH_INIT when that variable is set, else the released pool of the system, downloaded once.

fg.generate calls generate_timeline in timeline.py, which builds an IeeeSource and calls its generate. To generate on a grid that is not an IEEE case, build a SearchSource on its Network (Add a design family, an alarm rule or a test system).

docs.title: Where the code is
docs.text:
File Holds generation/source.py TimelineSource: the steps, written once generation/search.py SearchSource: coverage meters, search-based designs generation/ieee.py IeeeSource: a SearchSource for an IEEE case by name generation/plan.py the splits, the episode counts, the placement generation/design.py Designer, SplitDesign, the design processes generation/emit.py Walk: the frames, in time order generation/write.py TimelineWriter: the one writer of the file

Every source emits its scans through one generator, FdiaGenerator, in engine/:

File Holds engine/core.py FdiaGenerator: a Network, its meter plan and noise engine/base.py Part: one job of the generator, a class that holds the generator engine/measurement.py Emitter: a scan from a stored state engine/physics.py ScanLoads and LoadSplit: a scan's load and generation, read from its state

The attack designs are under engine/attacks/ (The attack families).

docs.title: Install and data versions
docs.text: The repository holds two distributions. fdia-graph generates a timeline and loads it. fdia-analysis runs estimators and localizers on one, and installs fdia-graph with it.

docs.title: The generation toolkit
docs.text:
Command Gives pip install fdia-graph the loader: opens a timeline and exports whole splits as numpy arrays pip install "fdia-graph[torch]" adds PyTorch: single records, batches and the DataLoader pip install "fdia-graph[pyg]" adds torch_geometric records and timelines pip install "fdia-graph[generate]" adds pandapower, to generate timelines pip install "fdia-graph[iso]" adds gridstatus, to download CAISO and ERCOT load profiles pip install "fdia-graph[ny]" adds what the New York build needs: pandapower and Pyomo pip install "fdia-graph[all]" every extra above

NYISO load profiles need no extra. The New York build also needs Ipopt, a solver that pip does not install: see Solving and Build the operating points.

docs.title: The analysis toolkit
docs.text: Command Gives pip install fdia-analysis the toolkit and fdia-graph: the threshold localizers and the results store pip install "fdia-analysis[se]" adds pandapower and scipy, for fdia_analysis.se and the residual localizer pip install "fdia-analysis[torch]" adds torch, for the learned localizers pip install "fdia-analysis[federated]" adds torch and scikit-learn, for fdia_analysis.federated pip install "fdia-analysis[all]" every analysis extra above

docs.title: Data versions
docs.text:
A released dataset belongs to a data release. Each package version pins one data release, so the same code always reads the same data.

  • fg.load("ieee118") reads the pinned release, or the one FDIA_GRAPH_RELEASE names when that variable is set.
  • fg.load("ieee118", release="v0.8.1") reads another one. Any timeline release from v0.8.0 can be read.
  • pip install --upgrade fdia-graph moves the pin forward when the new version pins a newer release.

docs.title: The cache
docs.text: A downloaded file is kept in ~/.cache/fdia_graph and is downloaded once. Set FDIA_GRAPH_CACHE to use another folder. After a download the package checks the file's sha256 for the releases v0.8.0, v0.8.1 and v0.8.3; a file of another release is not checked.

docs.title: Build the operating points
docs.text:
A timeline starts from a pool: one solved AC operating point per frame, in time order. This guide gets or builds the pool of a test system. Solving explains the two kinds of solve and the setting that chooses between them.

Paths are under src/fdia_graph/.

docs.title: What a pool is
docs.text:
Test system Pool Columns per bus IEEE case an array [T, N, 4] voltage (p.u.), P (MW), Q (MVAr), angle (deg) New York case a Pool record, in a file vm, va, p, q, with each frame's time

A pool holds the truth only. Meters, noise and attacks come later (Generate a timeline).

docs.title: An IEEE case: use the released pool
docs.text:
Each of the eight IEEE systems has a released pool of 72,000 operating points. fg.generate downloads it once and keeps it in the cache (Install and data versions). You do not build it.

import fdia_graph as fg

# downloads pool_ieee14.h5 (about 25 MB) on first use
fg.generate("ieee14", name="my_run", frames=2000)

The file is pool_ieee{N}.h5 with one dataset, X. The pool stores no timestamps. Frame t of a timeline is step t of its pool.

docs.title: An IEEE case: build your own pool
docs.text:
Three functions build a pool. All three are on the top-level package.

Function Does fg.fetch_profile downloads an operator's system load fg.load_profile reads a load series you already have fg.generate_states scales the case along the profile and solves each step

A profile is one number per step: the load series standardized to zero mean and unit variance.

import numpy as np

import fdia_graph as fg
from fdia_graph.data.profiles import RawSeries

# ten hours of a daily load curve, one value per minute
hours = np.arange(600) / 60.0
load_mw = 100 + 10 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * hours / 24)
profile = fg.load_profile(RawSeries(load_mw))

# needs fdia-graph[generate]
pool = fg.generate_states("ieee14", profile)
print(pool.shape)  # (600, 14, 4)

fg.generate("ieee14", name="own_pool", states=pool)

fg.load_profile takes one of three sources from data/profiles.py: RawSeries(values), CsvColumn(path, column) or IsoFolder(iso, directory).

fg.fetch_profile downloads a real load series instead:

profile = fg.fetch_profile(
    "nyiso", "2024-01-01", "2024-01-07", resample_min=1
)
iso Source Needs "nyiso" NYISO's public monthly archives nothing extra "caiso", "ercot" the gridstatus package fdia-graph[iso]

resample_min interpolates the series in time to that many minutes per step.

docs.title: What generate_states does at each step
docs.text:
Item Value Where Scale of a bus clip(1 + k S_t + j_t, 0.7, 1.3) _ar1_scale k 0.1 K_DEFAULT Jitter j_t AR(1) per bus, coefficient 0.98, standard deviation 0.03 LOAD_JITTER_RHO, SIGMA_DEFAULT What is scaled each load's P and Q and each generator's P _solve_states_chunk Solve AC power flow in pandapower _solve_states_chunk A step that fails dropped _solve_states_chunk

S_t is the profile at step t. The AR(1) jitter makes each bus drift smoothly from step to step and not jump. The clip holds every bus inside a plausible load band.

A shunt's draw is subtracted from the stored injections. The estimator models a shunt in the admittance matrix, not as an injection (_remove_shunt_injections).

generate_states takes workers=N to solve in N processes. A script that passes it must start under if __name__ == "__main__":.

docs.title: The solve setting
docs.text:
generate_states solves a power flow unless you pass solve=:

from fdia_graph.models.config import SolveSettings

by_opf = fg.generate_states(
    "ieee14",
    profile[:20],
    solve=SolveSettings(method="opf", engine="pandapower"),
)

With method="opf" each step scales the loads only and chooses the generator outputs by a least-cost AC OPF. engine="ipopt" runs the same problem in Ipopt. Solving lists every choice and which are refused.

docs.title: Your own pool file
docs.text:
states= of fg.generate takes an array or a path.

states Read as an array [T, N, 4] the pool itself a .npz file its array X a .h5 file its dataset X a folder files X_<t>.npy, one per step; more than 8,000 are read at an even stride

The column order is detected from the data: voltage is the only column whose every value is near 1.0. A pool in neither known order raises UnknownColumnOrder.

docs.title: The New York case: build the pool
docs.text: No New York pool is released. You build it from public inputs. The build scripts are in the repository's pipelines/newyork/, not in the wheel, so work from a checkout.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/myersben9/fdia-graph
pip install -e "./fdia-graph[ny]"
conda install -c conda-forge ipopt
export FG=$PWD/fdia-graph
  • The [ny] extra: pandapower, pandas, scipy, Pyomo, openpyxl and matpowercaseframes.
  • Ipopt, a solver that pip does not install (Solving).
  • A work folder for the inputs and the outputs. The scripts read data/ and write out/ relative to the folder you run them from.

docs.title: 1. Fetch the inputs
docs.text:
mkdir nygrid && cd nygrid
python -c "from fdia_graph.data.inputs import fetch_inputs; fetch_inputs('.')"

fetch_inputs in data/inputs.py writes data/:

Input Source NYgrid's Data/ folder the NYgrid repository at one pinned commit five-minute zone loads of 2019 NYISO's public archives utility service territories New York State Department of Public Service the location of each New York bus shipped with the package

A file that is already there is kept. The grid itself needs no download: it is the case file in the package (Test systems).

The load model downloads its own sources the first time a pool is built: building-stock load profiles, utility sales and industrial plant data. They are downloaded once and cached.

docs.title: 2. Run the pool
docs.text:
python $FG/pipelines/newyork/run_pool.py \
    2019-01-01 2020-01-01 out/pool_2019_v3.h5 --workers 4
Option Default Meaning START, END local-clock dates; END is not included OUT the pool file to write --workers 1 processes that solve the chunks --chunk-days 7 days per chunk --frames 0 stop after this many frames; 0 is all --seam-frames 288 most frames solved again at a seam --loads out/loads_2019_v2.npz the cached bus loads; built when missing --compare-hours off also print the dispatch cost against the hourly AC points

The year is 105,120 five-minute frames and takes several hours to solve. Try a week first:

python $FG/pipelines/newyork/run_pool.py \
    2019-01-07 2019-01-14 out/pool_week.h5 --workers 4

docs.title: What the script does
docs.text:
1. Loads. LoadModel (data/loads.py) builds a load for each New York bus at every frame.
  2. Hourly dispatch. read_nygrid (data/inputs.py) reads NYgrid's hourly data, and hourly_dispatch (data/dispatch.py) sets each hour's dispatch from it.
  3. Chunks. The window is cut into chunks, a week each by default, solved in parallel. PoolBuilder (data/pool.py) solves each chunk frame by frame: one OPF in Ipopt (IpoptSolver, data/ipopt_solver.py), then one power flow at its outputs (PandapowerSolver, data/pandapower_solver.py).
  4. Seams. The first frames of each chunk (at most --seam-frames) are solved again from the last state of the chunk before. They replace the stored frames up to the first frame where every thermal unit is within 0.5 MW of the stored dispatch. A seam that does not merge has its whole chunk solved again.
  5. The file. write_pool stores the pool.

PoolBuilder.from_settings takes a SolveSettings like generate_states. It builds by an OPF in Ipopt and refuses the other choices with the reason (Solving).

docs.title: Reading the pool back
docs.text:
from fdia_graph.constants.newyork import SolveKind
from fdia_graph.data.pool import read_pool

pool = read_pool("out/pool_2019_v3.h5")
solved = pool.solve_kind == SolveKind.SOLVED
print(solved.mean())

A frame that does not solve keeps its place with a NaN state, and only solved frames are used later. Troubleshooting lists the solve kinds.

Field of Pool Shape Holds time [T] each frame's time, NYISO's local clock vm, va [T, N] voltage magnitude (p.u.) and angle (deg) p, q [T, N] net injection (MW, MVAr) solve_kind [T] how the frame was solved (SolveKind) unit_p [T, G] each unit's dispatched output (MW)

docs.title: How the bus loads are built
docs.text:
LoadModel (data/loads.py) builds each New York load bus's profile bottom-up, by the method of [LI21]: prototype buildings and industrial plants, mixed by its utility's sector sales. The zone's real five-minute load is split over its buses in proportion to these profiles. Each bus then gets two terms of its own. Their constants are in constants/newyork.py.

Fluctuation (FLUCT_C, FLUCT_BETA, FLUCT_PHI). An AR(1) factor on the bus's load, p (1 + e).

  • e has standard deviation FLUCT_C size^-FLUCT_BETA, where size is the bus's mean load in MW. FLUCT_PHI is its AR(1) coefficient.
  • The term is the regulation component of ORNL/TM-2001/13.
  • The constants were fitted on the NYISO zones of 2018, with zone H left out.

Industrial switching (SWITCH_*). Pulses on a bus's industrial load.

  • The constants were fitted on zone D's five-minute steps of 2019 above 5 % of its mean load.
  • The number of pulses is a Poisson draw at SWITCH_RATE per MW of the bus's mean industrial load and hour.
  • A pulse's size, relative to the bus's mean industrial load, is the threshold SWITCH_U plus a generalized Pareto excess (shape SWITCH_XI, scale SWITCH_SCALE). A size above SWITCH_MAX is drawn again.
  • Its duration is lognormal (SWITCH_DUR_MU, SWITCH_DUR_SIGMA, log minutes).
  • A share SWITCH_OFF of pulses are drops. A drop is clipped so the load stays at or above zero.

Last, each zone's buses are rescaled to sum exactly to the zone's real load.

The fit functions are not part of the package.

docs.title: Where the code is
docs.text: File Holds data/profiles.py fetch_profile, load_profile and the load sources data/ieee_pool.py generate_states: the pool of an IEEE case data/inputs.py fetch_inputs and the readers of the New York inputs data/load_sources.py the building, sales and plant data, downloaded once data/loads.py LoadModel, LoadSeries: the New York bus loads data/dispatch.py Dispatch, hourly_dispatch data/config.py Settings of the New York build, and its random streams data/solver.py Solver: the interface of the two engines data/ipopt_solver.py IpoptSolver: the OPFs, in Pyomo with Ipopt data/pandapower_solver.py PandapowerSolver: the power flow, and pandapower's OPF data/ipopt.py ipopt: finds Ipopt and checks that it starts data/pool.py Pool, PoolBuilder, read_pool, write_pool

docs.title: Beating WLS: state estimation with the SDK
docs.text: Measurements in, state out, better than weighted least squares on the public test cases. Runs off the default timeline download (data release v0.8.3); pip install "fdia-analysis[se]".

docs.title: Baseline first
docs.text:
import fdia_graph as fg
from fdia_analysis.se.methods import WLS

train, test = fg.load("ieee14", split="train"), fg.load("ieee14", split="test")
wls = WLS().fit(train)
xhat = wls.estimate(test)  # [n, 2N-1] = [theta rad (non-slack) | V pu (all buses)]
print(wls.score(test).geo)  # angle_mae_deg, voltage_mae_pu (docs/analysis/estimation/README.md has the table)
fit() learns estimate() returns per-meter error scales: RMS of benign residuals at the dataset's clean truth (the benchmark default, calibrate="truth"), or each meter's accuracy class from measurements alone (calibrate="measured", what every detector path uses); the reference angle theta_ref the classical 2N-1 state, every voltage magnitude and every non-slack angle the chord Jacobian at the benign mean state in one angle frame: the slack angle is fixed to theta_ref, taken from the training truth at fit time (the case's reference angle on the released pools)

docs.title: The better estimator
docs.text:
from fdia_analysis.models.config import PriorConfig
from fdia_analysis.se.methods import SubspacePrior

est = SubspacePrior(prior=PriorConfig(rank_frac=0.2, reweight="huber", c=1.5)).fit(train)
print(est.score(test).geo)  # about half WLS's angle error on IEEE-14 (the table below)
piece does why it helps prior restricts the estimate to the low-rank subspace benign operation occupies (SVD of the training states) learns generator voltage setpoints from history instead of re-estimating them from noisy meters every scan Huber down-weights measurements the physics cannot explain rejects in-place meter corruption together on IEEE-14 test 45% lower angle error, 81% lower voltage error than WLS geometric mean over the eight record classes (benign and seven families), v0.8.3 timeline

Validation-selected hyperparameters from the estimation paper:

system rank_frac Huber c ResidualRemoval threshold ieee14 0.20 1.5 4.0 ieee118 0.50 2.5 5.0 ieee300 0.50 6.0 none helps

docs.title: PMU pseudo-measurements
docs.text:
On a hybrid-meter file (new generation) a SCADA voltmeter reads no angle, so the angle comes from the PMUs and the power meters alone. pmu_pseudo=True (every estimator, JacobianWeighting included, which reads the previous frame's currents from prev_pmu_i) adds the pseudo-measurements of [WU26, eq. (3)]: a PMU at the near end n of a branch reads V_n and I_n, and the branch's pi model gives the voltage at the far end f,

V_f = (I_n - y_nn V_n) / y_nf

with y_nn, y_nf the branch's Y_f or Y_t entries (taps and phase shifts included), averaged over the branches that reach f (formulas.estimation.pmu_pseudo_voltages). The pseudo |V| and angle fill the slots of the reached buses that no meter reads; a SCADA |V| is kept where one exists. Their first-order error, with independent PMU errors, is the covariance of

dV_f = R(1/y_nf) dI_n - R(y_nn/y_nf) P_n (d|V_n|, dtheta_n)

(R(c) the real 2x2 matrix of multiplying by c, P_n the polar-to-rectangular Jacobian at V_n), summed over the links with the voltage terms grouped by PMU bus, then carried to |V_f| and theta_f through the rectangular-to-polar gradients; for a round error of complex variance s^2 this is var|V_f| = s^2 / 2 and var theta_f = s^2 / (2 |V_f|^2). calibrate="measured" weights the pseudo slots by that variance, calibrate="truth" by their benign residual like every other slot. The formula is exact without noise (to 1e-16 on IEEE-14 and 118) and its variance matches a Monte Carlo of 20,000 draws to within 3% (analysis/tests/test_pmu_channels.py).

Measured with WLS on the test split, with only the meter model changed: taking the angles away from the SCADA voltmeters raises the benign angle error, and the eq. (3) pseudo-measurements win part of it back. The results store holds no run of this comparison, so this page gives no numbers for it.

docs.title: What to expect per family
docs.text:
records behaviour why At, Am (stealthy, and Aq, Al in older releases) robust weighting sees nothing; the prior moves them part of the way a consistent AC state leaves no residual, and it sits off the benign operating subspace, so the prior pulls the estimate part of the way back Ad bias, As scaling, Ar replay (older releases only) improve a lot meters corrupted in place, which robust weighting exists to reject benign improves on the larger systems, can lose slightly on ieee14 the baseline is already at the noise floor there

Full per-family table and figures, on data release v0.8.x: ../analysis/estimation/README.md.

docs.title: Your own estimator
docs.text:
Subclass SEBase and override one hook; the rest is shared, so comparisons are estimator against estimator.

hook does _fit_states(x_benign) learn anything from the benign training states _subspace() a [2N-1, K] basis that restricts the state space, or None for the full state _solve(z, w) the per-batch solve; w is per-record weights [n, m], or None for the shared ones

Inside _solve: self._w_solve(z, w) is the divergence-guarded weighted iteration, self._nres(x, z) the normalized residuals, and formulas.estimation holds every equation (huber_weights, wls_step, normalized_residual, ...).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Every stage either raises a named error or records why it produced less than asked. This page lists what each stage reports, what it means and what to do. It covers every test system; a row that applies to one system says so.

docs.title: The kinds of error
docs.text:
The named errors of the package are defined in src/fdia_graph/errors.py. A few conditions raise a built-in error: a missing optional package (ImportError), an unknown dataset name (KeyError), a missing or corrupt download (FileNotFoundError, OSError), and an IEEE pool with no converged step (RuntimeError).

Error Means Is a ConfigError an argument or a setting has a value its model does not allow ValueError DataConditionError the data read does not meet a condition ValueError SolverUnavailable the environment cannot run the solver RuntimeError

The other named errors are subclasses of DataConditionError, except MissingCapability, which is a ConfigError. So except ValueError catches every named error but SolverUnavailable. A broken environment is not a property of the data.

A settings model checks its values when it is built, before any download or file is made. The message names the field and what it may be.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
What you see Why Fix SolverUnavailable: Pyomo is not installed the [ny] extra is missing pip install "fdia-graph[ny]" SolverUnavailable: Ipopt is not found or does not start Ipopt is not installed, or cannot load its DLLs see below ImportError for pandapower the [generate] extra is missing pip install "fdia-graph[generate]" a change you made does not show up Python imports another copy of the package put your checkout's src first on PYTHONPATH a script starts itself again and again it asks for several workers without a main guard start it under if __name__ == "__main__":

Ipopt. Install it with conda install -c conda-forge ipopt into the environment, and run that environment's Python with the environment active. On Windows a missing DLL shows as exit code 0xC0000135. fdia_graph.data.ipopt.ipopt() adds the environment's Library/bin folder to PATH when it exists. Check it:

from fdia_graph.data.ipopt import ipopt

print(ipopt().version())

Another copy of the package. This usually happens in a git worktree, when an editable install points at the main checkout.

Workers. The design processes and the pool workers are spawned, and a spawned process imports the script that started it.

docs.title: Loading a dataset
docs.text: What you see Why Fix NotATimeline the file's kind is not timeline: an older record shard, or another file load a release from v0.8.0 on NotATimeline from Dataset the file does not record its clients open it with fg.FdiaGraph, or generate it with own= MissingCapability the view lacks what the caller needs, for example PMU currents load a file that has them ConfigError on fg.load an option is not one of its choices the message lists the choices

docs.title: The operating points
docs.text:
An IEEE case (fg.generate_states, fg.generate):

What you see Why Fix RuntimeError: no operating points converged no step's power flow converged check the profile and the scaling arguments DataConditionError from an OPF pool no step has an optimum within the case's limits use a power flow, or another case (Solving) ConfigError on SolveSettings a power flow in Ipopt pandapower runs every power flow UnknownColumnOrder the pool's column order cannot be read from its values store the columns as voltage, P, Q, angle

The New York case (pipelines/newyork/run_pool.py):

What you see Why Fix FileNotFoundError on data/... the scripts read data/ and out/ relative to the working folder run from the work folder that holds data/ DataConditionError: bus ... has no row in ... a bus has no location in the bus-location table fetch the inputs again (fetch_inputs in data/inputs.py) DataConditionError: ... first hour has no AC point the span's first hour did not solve, so the chunk has no start start the span at another hour ConfigError on PoolBuilder.from_settings a solve choice the New York pool cannot be built with Solving

PoolBuilder.report() counts every frame by its solve kind. Only solved frames are used later.

Solve kind Meaning What to do solved the dispatch and the power flow converged nothing failed one of them did not converge the frame is kept in place and counted by report(); many in a row point at the inputs of those hours no_hour the hour the chunk starts from has no AC point rebuild that span no_load NYISO has no load for the frame: the spring-forward gap, or a gap in its data nothing; nothing is solved for these frames

report() before build() raises NotFitted.

docs.title: Any test system
docs.text:
What you see Why Fix ConfigError: generate_timeline got unknown settings a keyword that is no setting the settings tables a ConfigError saying the pool carries no time split_by="week" on a pool without times pass time=, or use split_by="time" a ConfigError about SplitRule.time the times are not one datetime64 per frame, increasing split_by and time= a RuntimeWarning that a split's placements jammed the split could not fit every episode; one was dropped lower attacked_frac, shorten the episodes, or use more frames a RuntimeWarning that an episode found no feasible design it had no design after 20 moves (REDRAWS) see below; the file records the shortfall no file after a failed run the file is written under a .part name and renamed only when whole fix the error and run again

A file records what it could not build, per split and family, in the attributes episodes_requested, episodes_built, episode_redraws, episodes_dropped and episode_shortfall. fallback_benign counts the frames of an episode stored benign.

docs.title: A SearchSource
docs.text:
What you see Why Fix NoAdmissibleTarget a family has nothing to attack on this case drop the family, or check max_load_mw NoLineRatings am_attack=OverloadSettings(rating_source="pglib") on a case without PGLib-OPF ratings use rating_source="pool" ConfigError: ... generates one timeline a second generate on one source build a new source ConfigError: ... the generator makes At, Am only families names an older family use At and Am

An overload window with no stealthy design is moved to another onset of its split. The measured IEEE-14 builds record their redraws and one shortfall (Generate a timeline).

docs.title: A design family of your own
docs.text:
A family that subclasses AttackFamily can say why a design found no attack (design_explained in engine/attacks/family.py). After source.generate(path), source.designer.log holds every design attempt of the run, each with its miss reason (Tried.miss). A slot is tried again at every onset it moves to, so the log counts attempts, not slots.

Miss reason Meaning no_target the family set last_miss to it: the window held nothing to attack infeasible the family returned None and gave no reason solver_error the family raised its solver_errors count during the design, so infeasible may be wrong

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: What you see Why Fix NoBenignRecords a fit that calibrates on benign records was given none pass the train split unfiltered NoAttackedRecords a threshold tuned on validation records was given no attacked ones pass a validation split that has both NotFitted a step that needs an earlier one was called first call the earlier step SlackMismatch the dataset's slack bus is not the case's use the dataset of that case VaryingReference the slack angle varies across the training frames there is no one reference angle to fix MissingCapability on pmu_pseudo the file has no PMU currents use a file generated with the hybrid meters NoSuchResult a results query found no record, or several check the query's filters

docs.title: Check the package yourself
docs.text: This page lists what the package claims and the test that checks each claim. Run a test to see the claim hold on your machine. Read the test to see exactly what is compared: each row says the case the test runs on and the tolerance it uses.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
Work from a checkout, because the tests are not in the wheel.

git clone https://github.com/myersben9/fdia-graph
cd fdia-graph
pip install -e ".[generate,test]" -e "./analysis[test]"

Run one test by its name:

python -m pytest -q tests/test_timeline.py::test_a_stealthy_frame_is_the_benign_scan_plus_its_attack_vector

Run everything the install above can run (it downloads the IEEE pools it needs, once):

python -m pytest -q -n 4 -rs tests analysis/tests

-rs lists each skipped test with its reason. The "Needs" column below says what a test needs beyond the install above.

Without it the whole folder tests/nygrid is left out of the run, and asking for one of its tests by name reports "not found" Ipopt also the Ipopt solver on your PATH (what to install). docs.title: What these tests do not show
docs.text:
• Byte identity across platforms. The stored digests are compared bit for bit only on the platform they were recorded on (tests/digests.py). Elsewhere those tests are skipped, and the other tests on this page still run.
  • A New York pool build on every platform. It repeats bit for bit on some platforms and only to a tolerance on others (Repeating a solve).
  • The released data files. A download checks the sha256 of the releases the package lists (src/fdia_graph/download.py). No test rebuilds a released file.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Per-record timings on the tiny IEEE-14 timeline, stored by python tools/bench.py as a run of the results store's bench experiment (results/bench.csv) and rendered below by tools/results_docs.py; --check fails when a timing is more than 3x slower than the last run. One machine's rows are comparable with each other, not with another machine's.

From 0.18 the generate column is milliseconds per timeline frame of the test suite's tiny timeline (TIMELINE_KW in tests/helpers.py, 1000 frames); earlier rows timed the record-shard writer per record and are not comparable to it.

From 0.20 that timeline has one-frame Aq and Al episodes, and its seed moved with them, so a later row's generate column times a different episode mix from the rows above it. From 0.21 it holds At and the overload Am only on the hybrid meters (seed 2, the search capped at 16 supports): other frames and another meter plan, so none of its columns, the estimators' included, compares with the rows above. tools/bench.py records the fixture recipe with each row, starts a new table for a new recipe, and --check compares only rows of the same machine and recipe; the first run on this recipe starts its baseline.

Every episode returned the same answer before and after.

The search speed-up:
